docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Pantheon is a set of user interface components for Roblox. It is built on Fusion 0.3. It has about 70 components, a light and a dark theme, and a separate set for game HUDs.

Get started Using Pantheon

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Theming

    Components take their colours, fonts and spacing from a theme. Change the theme and every component changes with it. Light and dark themes are included.

    Theming

  • State that survives a rebuild

    Controls can keep what the user entered when you rebuild the interface. This means you can change the theme or the layout without losing anything.

    Persisting state

  • Accessibility

    Components follow the player's settings for reduced motion, transparency and text size. Controls work with a keyboard or a gamepad.

    Accessibility

  • Game components

    A hotbar with an inventory panel, a backpack, a leaderboard and a top bar. They are styled for games and do not use the app theme.

    Hotbar

  • DevTools

    A panel for inspecting an interface while it runs. You can browse the element tree and change properties.

    DevTools

  • Built with Fusion

    You can give most properties a Fusion state. The component updates when the state changes. If you give a control a Value, the control and the Value stay in step both ways.

    Common properties

docs.title: A first look
docs.text:
local Pantheon = require(Packages.Pantheon)
local C = Pantheon.Components

local scope = Pantheon.scoped()
local theme = Pantheon.Theme.create("Light")

Pantheon.Theme.Provide(theme, function()
    C.Button(scope, {
        Text = "Run",
        Variant = "Filled",
        OnClick = function()
            print("Running")
        end,
    })
end)

docs.title: Alert
docs.text: Alert is a banner that gives the user a message. Its colour shows how serious the message is.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Alert with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Alert(scope, {
    Title = "Heads up",
    Text = "Your session expires in five minutes.",
    Tone = "Warning", -- (1)!
})
  1. Tone is "Info", "Success", "Warning" or "Error".

docs.title: Loader
docs.text: Loader is a set of loading animations. Choose one with Kind. All of them are square, so they fit the same layouts.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Loader with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Loader(scope, { Kind = "Orbit", SizePx = 36 })
C.Loader(scope, { Kind = "Icon", Icon = "refresh-cw", Motion = "Spin" })

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text: Kind Description "Beachball" A spinning rainbow pinwheel, as on macOS. "Dots" Three bouncing dots. "Bars" Bars that move up and down like an equaliser. "Ripple" Rings that spread out from a dot in the middle. "Orbit" Dots that chase each other around a circle. "Gnome" A thin ring with a small dot circling it, with a fading trail. "Icon" A Lucide icon with a motion: "Spin", "Pulse", "Bounce", "Flip" or "Wiggle".

docs.title: Conical gradients
docs.text: The beachball uses a conical UIGradient if the engine supports it. If not, it uses stacked discs. See Flags.

docs.title: LoadingIndicator
docs.text: LoadingIndicator is the loading shape from Material 3 Expressive. It is a solid shape that spins and changes through a cycle of other shapes.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.LoadingIndicator with a scope and a table of properties:

C.LoadingIndicator(scope, { SizePx = 56, Contained = true })

docs.title: How it is drawn
docs.text: Roblox has no polygon element. Each shape is cut into horizontal strips, with up to two spans in each strip so that notches and lobes stay. Changing shape moves the edges of each strip. The strips have one colour and spin together, so they look like one shape.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text: Oval, Pill, Triangle, Arrow, Fan, Diamond, Clamshell, Pentagon, Gem, Sunny, VerySunny, SoftBurst, Cookie4, Cookie6, Cookie7, Cookie9, Cookie12 and Burst. The default cycle is the one in the Material 3 specification.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text: Progress shows how far a task has got, as a bar or a ring. If you do not set a Value, it is indeterminate: it shows that something is happening but not how much is done.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Progress with a scope and a table of properties:

local done = scope:Value(0.4)

C.Progress(scope, { Value = done }) -- bar
C.Progress(scope, { Variant = "Circular", Value = done, SizePx = 48 })
C.Progress(scope, { Variant = "Circular" }) -- (1)!
  1. With no Value, a circular progress is the LoadingIndicator, which changes shape. Set Indicator to "Arc" for a spinning arc.

docs.title: Snackbar
docs.text: Snackbar is a short message on a surface that contrasts with the app. It can have an icon or element before the message, an action, an element after it, and a close button. To show messages that appear and disappear, use SnackbarHost.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Snackbar with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Snackbar(scope, {
    Message = "Message deleted",
    Icon = "trash-2",
    ActionText = "Undo",
    OnAction = function()
        print("Restored")
    end,
    Dismissible = true, -- (1)!
    OnDismiss = function()
        print("Closed")
    end,
})
  1. Dismissible adds a close button at the end. The snackbar does not remove itself, so remove it in OnDismiss. SnackbarHost removes its messages for you.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: From the start, the parts are: Leading or Icon, the message, the action button, Trailing, and the close button. Use Leading and Trailing to add your own elements, such as an avatar or a spinner.

ZIndex UsedAs<number> - Z index of the component. Message UsedAs<string> - The message. ActionText string - Label of the action button. If you leave it out, there is no button.

docs.title: SnackbarHost
docs.text: SnackbarHost shows toasts as a stack. The newest is in front and the ones before it peek out behind. Move the pointer over the stack and it spreads out so you can read every toast. It does not return an instance: it returns a table with a Show function that adds a toast and a Clear function that removes them all.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.SnackbarHost with a scope and a table of properties:

local toasts = C.SnackbarHost(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer,
    MaxVisible = 5,
})

local dismiss = toasts.Show("Saved", "Undo", function()
    print("Undone")
end, {
    Icon = "check",
    Dismissible = true, -- (1)!
    Duration = 5,
})

dismiss() -- (2)!
  1. Dismissible adds a close button to the toast.
  2. Show returns a function that dismisses only that toast.

docs.title: The stack
docs.text:
While the stack is closed, the newest toast is in front at full size. Each older toast is a little narrower and sits a little higher behind it, and its text is hidden so it reads as a shape. Only the three toasts at the front are shown, and the rest fade out of view.

When the pointer is over the stack or next to it, the toasts spread out into a column and their timers stop. When the pointer leaves, the stack closes and the timers start again.

docs.title: Adding to a toast
docs.text:
Leading and Trailing in the options add your own elements before the message and after the action button. Give an element, or a function that builds one. A function is called with the scope of the toast, so what it creates is cleaned up with it, and with a function that dismisses the toast:

toasts.Show("Uploading", nil, nil, {
    Duration = math.huge,
    Trailing = function(toastScope, dismiss)
        return C.Button(toastScope, { Text = "Cancel", OnClick = dismiss })
    end,
})

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text: The host is mounted on Layer, or on a layer set with Layer.Provide or Layer.bind. Without either, parent Instance yourself.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Name Type Required Default Description MaxVisible number 5 Most toasts kept at once. The oldest is dismissed past that. Width number 360 Width of the stack in pixels.

For a ring that fills up as a task progresses, use Progress with Variant = "Circular".

docs.title: Checkbox
docs.text:
Note

Use a Checkbox when the user chooses items from a list. Use a Switch for a setting that takes effect immediately.

Checkbox lets the user turn one option on or off. The check mark is drawn in two strokes.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Checkbox with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Checkbox(scope, {
    Label = "Remember me",
    Checked = true,
    OnChanged = function(checked)

    end,
})

docs.title: NumberField
docs.text: NumberField is a text box for a number. The label at the start is a scrub handle. Drag it sideways to change the value without typing.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.NumberField with a scope and a table of properties:

local x = scope:Value(0)

C.NumberField(scope, {
    Label = "X", -- (1)!
    Value = x,
    Step = 1,
    Suffix = "px",
})
  1. The label is the scrub handle. If you do not set a Label, the user can only type in the field.

docs.title: Scrubbing
docs.text:
Drag the label to change the value. Hold Shift to change it 10 times faster, or Alt to change it 10 times slower. If the user presses the label without moving, the text box takes focus.

If you set both Min and Max, the speed is the range divided by 300 pixels. Otherwise the value changes by one step for every 4 pixels. Set ScrubSpeed to choose the speed yourself.

docs.title: Typing
docs.text: Type a number and press Enter, or click away, to confirm it. If the text is not a number, the field goes back to the old value. While the box has focus, the Up and Down arrow keys change the value by Step. Shift and Alt change the speed in the same way.

docs.title: NumberSpinner
docs.text: NumberSpinner shows a number and animates it when the number changes. It follows the style of contentTransition(.numericText()) in SwiftUI. By default, a digit that changes slides, shrinks and blurs out while the new digit comes in.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.NumberSpinner with a scope and a table of properties:

local count = scope:Value(1280)

C.NumberSpinner(scope, {
    Value = count, -- (1)!
    Prefix = "$",
    Decimals = 2,
    TextSize = 36,
})

count:set(1534.5)
  1. Value is a state. The digits animate each time it changes.

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
With Style set to "Numeric", the default, each digit animates on its own. The columns start one after another, from left to right. The timing is based on measurements of the iOS animation, with more overshoot. Use Speed and Bounce to change it.

With Style set to "Roll", each digit turns like an odometer wheel, through every digit between the old value and the new one. Use SpringSpeed and SpringDamping to change the spring.

docs.title: Size
docs.text: The box has a fixed width, so the layout does not move when the number changes. Digits sets how many whole-number digits fit. The default is the number of digits in the starting value plus one, and at least four. Set Width to choose the width yourself.

docs.title: DockPanel
docs.text: DockPanel is a panel with a header, for the docked areas of a tool. The header has a title or a row of tabs, and actions. The panel can collapse to its header.

C.DockPanel(scope, {

        { Id = "attrs", Title = "Attributes", Content = attributesView },

docs.title: Tabs or a title

docs.text: With Collapsible, an arrow at the start of the header collapses the panel to the height of the header, and its content fades out. The panel shrinks from the Size you gave it. Use it in a layout that lets the neighbours take the freed space, such as a list layout.

docs.title: Explorer
docs.text: Explorer shows a tree of Instances, like the Explorer window of Studio. You can expand and collapse branches, filter, select several rows, rename and drag one instance onto another.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Explorer with a scope and a table of properties:

local filter = scope:Value("")
local picked = scope:Value({})

C.Explorer(scope, {
    Roots = { workspace, game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage") },
    Filter = filter,
    Selected = picked,
    AllowReparent = true,
    OnActivate = function(instance)
        print("Open", instance:GetFullName())
    end,
})

docs.title: Rows
docs.text: Each row has an arrow, an icon for the class and the name. The list is built from the instances that are showing, so a tree of any size scrolls through a VirtualList. The list follows the tree: instances that are added, removed or renamed appear in it.

docs.title: Selecting
docs.text: A press selects a row. Hold Ctrl to add or remove one, or Shift to select the rows from the last one pressed. Two quick presses call OnActivate.

docs.title: Keyboard
docs.text:
Focus the Explorer with Tab. Then:

  • Up and Down move the selection.
  • Right opens a branch, or moves to its first child. Left closes it, or moves to its parent.
  • Enter calls OnActivate.
  • F2 renames the selected instance. Enter commits and Escape cancels.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text: With a Filter, the tree shows the instances whose name contains the text, and the branches that lead to them. Branches with a match are open. Match lets you match on more than the name, for example the class.

docs.title: Reparenting
docs.text: With AllowReparent, drag a row onto another to make it the parent. An instance is never dropped onto itself or onto something inside it. Without OnReparent, the component sets Parent itself.

docs.title: ScrollArea
docs.text: ScrollArea is a scrolling container with its own scroll bar. It scrolls with the mouse wheel and keeps moving after a flick. It stretches past the edge and springs back. You can run an action when the user pulls past the top, for example to refresh.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.ScrollArea with a scope and a table of properties:

C.ScrollArea(scope, {
    Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1),
    Children = {
        C.Text(scope, { Text = "Long content" }),
    },
    OnRefresh = function() -- (1)!
        reload()
    end,
})
  1. OnRefresh is called when the user pulls past the top and lets go. While the user pulls, a hint shows what will happen. It is not limited to refreshing.

docs.title: Controls inside a scroll area
docs.text: A control inside the area that follows a drag, such as a slider or a colour picker, keeps the drag to itself. The area does not scroll along with it.

docs.title: Virtual content
docs.text: To show a very long list, use VirtualList, which is built on ScrollArea. Set ContentLayout = "None" and ContentPadding = 0 if you place content yourself.

docs.title: VirtualList
docs.text:
Note

All rows have the same height. A row is built when it comes into range and is not rebuilt when the data changes, so read state inside the row instead of building it from a plain value.

VirtualList shows a long list by building only the rows that are on screen, plus a few either side. It is a ScrollArea, so it scrolls the same way.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.VirtualList with a scope and a table of properties:

C.VirtualList(scope, {
    Size = UDim2.new(1, 0, 0, 240),
    ItemCount = #names,
    ItemHeight = 40,
    RenderItem = function(rowScope, index) -- (1)!
        return C.ListItem(rowScope, { Title = names[index] })
    end,
})
  1. RenderItem gets a scope for the row and the index of the row. The scope is destroyed when the row scrolls out of range, so create everything for the row in it. Do not use the main scope.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text: Toolbar is a bar of tool buttons. A button can be a toggle, show a tooltip with its shortcut, and be disabled. Separators group the buttons.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:

C.Toolbar(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer, -- (1)!
    Items = {
        { Id = "select", Icon = "mouse-pointer", Tooltip = "Select", Shortcut = "V", Toggle = true, Toggled = true },
        { Id = "move", Icon = "move-3d", Tooltip = "Move", Shortcut = "W", Toggle = true },
        { Separator = true },
        { Id = "snap", Icon = "sliders-horizontal", Text = "Snap", Toggle = true, Toggled = snap },
        { Spacer = true },

docs.title: Window
docs.text: Window is a rounded app shell. It holds an app bar, a navigation rail, the content and a layer for overlays. It can be dragged by its app bar and resized from its edges.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Window with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Window(scope, {
    Size = scope:Value(UDim2.fromOffset(640, 420)), -- (1)!
    Position = scope:Value(UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5)),
    AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5),
    Draggable = true,
    Resizable = true,
    AppBar = C.AppBar(scope, { Title = "Catalog" }),
    NavigationRail = C.NavigationRail(scope, { Items = items }),
    Overlays = { overlayLayer }, -- (2)!
    Children = { content },
})
  1. Pass a Value as Size or Position and the window writes to it while it is dragged or resized, so the result survives a rebuild.
  2. Anything that floats, such as popovers, tooltips, dialogs and toasts, should be mounted on a layer inside the window. It then moves with the window and follows its rounded corners. See Overlay layers.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
With a vertical rail, the rail runs the full height of the window. The app bar sits beside it and the content below the app bar. The rail is drawn above the app bar so its shadow falls on it. With a horizontal rail, the app bar is at the top and the rail along the bottom.

A window cannot clip to rounded corners, so the app bar and the rail round their own corners to match the window: with a vertical rail the rail takes the two left corners and the app bar the top right.

docs.title: Dragging
docs.text: The window is dragged by its app bar. DragBounds decides how far it may go off screen.

docs.title: Resizing
docs.text: Set Resizable to add handles on the edges and corners. Use MinSize, MaxSize, ResizeRatio and ResizeSnap to limit the size. OnResized is called on every step.

docs.title: Coachmark
docs.text: Coachmark points at an element to introduce it. It dims everything else, cuts a hole around the element, rings it with a pulse and shows a card with some text and a button.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Coachmark with a scope and a table of properties:

local open = scope:Value(true)

    Target = newButton,

    Title = "Try this first",
    Text = "The new button starts a project.",

    Title = "Delete file?",

docs.title: Menu
docs.text: Menu is a panel of rows. It can be a flat list, have groups with titles, and have pages that slide in and out for submenus. Give it data with Items or Sections, or build it from MenuSection, MenuButton and MenuPage.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.Menu with a scope and a table of properties:

C.Menu(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer,
    Open = open,
    Sections = {
        {
            Title = "Edit",
            Items = {
                { Text = "Copy", Icon = "copy" },
                { Text = "Paste", Icon = "clipboard" },
            },
        },
    },
    OnClose = function()
        open:set(false)
    end,
})

docs.title: RadialMenu
docs.text: RadialMenu shows a ring of choices around the pointer, as in the emote wheel of many games. Point in the direction of a choice and release the key, or click it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.RadialMenu with a scope and a table of properties:

C.RadialMenu(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer,
    Hotkey = Enum.KeyCode.Q, -- (1)!
    Title = "Emote",
    Items = {

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:

With a gamepad, push the left thumbstick toward a choice and press A. B closes the ring, and so does Escape.

docs.title: ColorPicker
docs.text: ColorPicker chooses one colour. It has three tabs: swatches, a saturation and brightness square with a hue slider, and sliders for each channel of a colour model. GradientPicker uses it to edit the stops of a gradient.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.ColorPicker with a scope and a table of properties:

local color = scope:Value(Color3.fromRGB(0, 105, 92))

C.ColorPicker(scope, {
    Value = color, -- (1)!
    OnChange = function(newColor, alpha)
        print(newColor, alpha)
    end,
})
  1. Value is a Color3 or a Value<Color3>. A Value and the picker follow each other: setting the state moves the picker, and moving the picker sets the state.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
• Grid shows swatches. Palette replaces them.
  • Spectrum is a saturation and brightness square with a hue slider. With Area = "Wheel" it is a hue ring around the square instead. The ring needs conical gradients and falls back to the square without them.
  • Sliders has one slider for each channel of a model: "RGB", "HSB" (also "HSV"), "HSL", "LAB" or "Hex". The models show as chips under the tabs.

docs.title: Sliders and thumbs
docs.text: Each slider is filled with the gradient of its channel and has a number field. The thumb is small at rest and grows to the height of the track while it is pressed. The handles on the square and the ring behave the same way.

docs.title: Alpha
docs.text: There is an alpha slider over a checkerboard on every tab. Set ShowAlpha = false to remove it.

docs.title: CurveEditor
docs.text: CurveEditor edits a NumberSequence, the curve used by particles, beams and trails. It is a plot of a smooth curve with keypoints you can drag, tangent handles to shape it, and number fields for the selected keypoint.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.CurveEditor with a scope and a table of properties:

local curve = scope:Value(NumberSequence.new(0, 1))

C.CurveEditor(scope, {
    Value = curve, -- (1)!
    Min = 0,
    Max = 1,
    ShowEnvelope = true,
})
  1. A Value and the editor follow each other. Assign curve:get() to a ParticleEmitter.Size, for example. A NumberSequence is a list of straight pieces, so the curve is sampled into up to 20 keypoints, spread over the curved segments.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
• Drag a keypoint to move it. The first keypoint stays at time 0 and the last at time 1, and a keypoint cannot pass its neighbours.
  • Select a keypoint to show its two tangent handles (the diamonds). Drag one to bend the curve. Keypoints you have not shaped get smooth tangents that follow their neighbours and stay flat at peaks.
  • Double click the plot to add a keypoint. It starts on the curve and splits it where it is, so the curve does not change.
  • Select a keypoint and press the trash button, or focus it and press Delete, to remove it. The first and last keypoints cannot be removed.
  • The fields under the plot edit the selected keypoint: T is its time, V its value and ± its envelope, when ShowEnvelope is on.
  • A focused keypoint moves with the arrow keys.

docs.title: GradientPicker
docs.text: GradientPicker edits a gradient with any number of colour stops. A ColorPicker below the editor changes the colour of the selected stop.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Components.GradientPicker with a scope and a table of properties:

local preview = scope:New("UIGradient")({})

C.GradientPicker(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer, -- (1)!
    OnGradientChanged = function(colors, transparency, rotation, offset)
        preview.Color = colors
        preview.Transparency = transparency
        preview.Rotation = rotation
        preview.Offset = offset
    end,
})
  1. Layer is where the tooltips of the buttons are mounted. Without it, or a layer set with Layer.Provide or Layer.bind, there are no tooltips.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
The top container holds the gradient bar and the controls for the selected stop:

  • Bar. Press a handle to select it and drag it along the bar. Press an empty part of the bar to add a stop there, coloured from the gradient at that point. Handles scale in when they are added, and the selected one is slightly larger and grows while it is dragged.
  • Rot, Pos and Alpha. Three boxes in a row. Press one and it grows to fill the row, while the others fade out and its editor fades in. The editor has a back arrow, a slider and a text field. Rot is the rotation of the gradient. Pos is its offset, with an X row and a Y row. Alpha is the opacity of the selected stop.
  • Hex. The hex colour of the selected stop, with buttons to duplicate and to delete it. A gradient keeps at least two stops, so delete is disabled at two.

docs.title: The node editor
docs.text: Under the editor, on a darker fill with no gap between them, is a plain ColorPicker with no footer and no alpha slider. It edits the colour of the selected stop. Its tabs, models and swatches are the same as the static picker, and Modes, Models, Mode, Model, Area and Palette are passed on to it.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: OnGradientChanged is called with values that can be assigned straight to a UIGradient: a ColorSequence for Color, a NumberSequence for Transparency, a number for Rotation and a Vector2 for Offset. It is called once when the picker is created, so a preview is right before the first edit.

docs.title: Backpack
docs.text: Backpack feeds a Hotbar from the Roblox backpack of a player, so a game does not need its own inventory. It follows the tools in the backpack and the tool the character is holding.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Game.Backpack with a scope and optional settings. It returns the properties to give to a Hotbar:

local Game = Pantheon.Game

local inventory = Game.Backpack(scope, { Capacity = 27 })

Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = inventory.Items,
    Selected = inventory.Selected,
    OnSelect = inventory.OnSelect,
    OnMove = inventory.OnMove,
    Capacity = 27,
})

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
• A tool takes the first free slot when it arrives.
  • Equipping a slot with the bar equips that tool, and unequipping calls UnequipTools. If you equip or unequip a tool another way, Selected follows.
  • A tool moves between the backpack and the character when it is equipped. The bar only forgets a tool once it is in neither.
  • The item for a tool has the Name of the tool, its ToolTip as the Description, its TextureId as the Image, and the tool itself as Tool. The name, tooltip and texture are watched, so a change shows on the bar.

docs.title: Hotbar
docs.text: Hotbar is an inventory bar for a game. The number keys equip the slots, items can be dragged between slots, and the backtick key opens the whole inventory in a searchable panel above the bar. It can use your own inventory data or the Roblox backpack.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Pantheon.Game.Hotbar with a scope and a table of properties:

local Game = Pantheon.Game

local items = scope:Value({
    [1] = { Name = "Sword", Description = "Starter blade", Tags = { "weapon" } },
    [2] = { Name = "Bow", Count = 24 },
    [11] = { Name = "Torch" },
})

Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 1),
    Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 1, -16),
    Items = items, -- (1)!
    Slots = 9,
    Capacity = 27,
    OnSelect = function(slot)
        print("Equipped slot", slot)
    end,
})
  1. Items is a table from slot number to item. Pass a Value and a drag writes the new order back to it. Otherwise handle OnMove.

docs.title: Items
docs.text:
An item is a table with these fields:

Field Type Description Name string? Name shown in the tooltip. Without an Image, its first two letters are drawn on the slot. Description string? Second line of the tooltip. Image string? Asset ID of the icon. Count number? Stack size, shown on the slot when it is above 1. Cooldown number or State<number> Part of the cooldown that is left, from 0 to 1. It draws as a block that shrinks down the slot. Id, Tags string, { string } Extra names the search can match.

Other string fields are searchable too.

docs.title: Using the bar
docs.text:
• The number keys 1 to 9 and 0 equip the slot, and pressing the same key again unequips it. Set BindKeys = false to handle keys yourself.
  • A click equips a slot. Press and drag past a few pixels to pick an item up, and drop it on another slot to swap the two. The equipped item stays with its item.
  • The equipped slot turns white with dark content and casts a shadow. A dragged item casts a larger one.
  • A slot grows a little when hovered and shows the name and description of its item.

docs.title: Slots that have no item
docs.text:
Empty slots are hidden and the bar closes up around the items. They come back while you drag, so you can drop an item on one, and while the inventory is open.

An item that arrives slides up from below, scales up and fades in. A removed item keeps sliding up, scales down and fades out. The space it takes in the bar opens straight away and closes only after the exit animation, so neighbouring slots never overlap.

docs.title: The inventory panel
docs.text: The backtick key opens a panel above the bar. It scales up and slides up as it fades in. It holds a search box and a grid of every slot beyond the bar. The grid is a VirtualList in a ScrollArea, so only the rows in view are built, and it scrolls once it is taller than ExpandedRows. The bar shows all its slots, numbered, while the panel is open. Pass a Value as Expanded to open and close it from code.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
The search box is a TextField. It filters the grid with a fuzzy match, so hlng finds Healing Potion, and orders the results by how well they match.

A word is matched against the name, the description, the Id, the Tags and any other string field of the item. To match only one of them, write scope:text, for example name:bow. Add your own scopes with SearchScopes:

Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    SearchScopes = {
        type = function(item)
            return item.Type
        end,
    },
})

A scope returns a string, or a list of strings, for an item. A search for type:weapon then matches those items, and weapon alone matches them too.

docs.title: Roblox backpack
docs.text: Game.Hotbar does not need a custom inventory. Backpack turns the tools of a player into the Items, Selected, OnSelect and OnMove that the bar needs. The default Roblox backpack is hidden while the bar exists, and shown again when the scope is destroyed. Set DisableDefault = false to keep it.

docs.title: Leaderboard
docs.text: Leaderboard is a player list in the style of the one in Roblox: translucent rows with a faded headshot, a display name that gives way to the username when you hover, and team headers that fold their players away. Players can join and leave with an animation, and the whole list can slide off the screen.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Call Pantheon.Game.Leaderboard with a scope and a table of properties:

local Game = Pantheon.Game

Game.Leaderboard(scope, {
    Title = "Players",
    Self = localUserId,
    Sort = "Value",
    Teams = {
        {
            Name = "Red",
            Color = Color3.fromRGB(196, 40, 28),
            Players = {
                { Id = 1, Name = "ada_l", DisplayName = "Ada", UserId = 1, Value = 4200 },
            },
        },
    },
})

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
A row is a table with these fields:

Field Type Description Id any Identifies the row. Keep it between updates, so the row is not rebuilt. Name string The username. It is shown as @Name when the row is hovered. DisplayName string? The name shown at rest. It is Name when left out. UserId number? The Roblox user id, for the headshot. Image string? An asset ID for a picture, for a row that is not a Roblox user. It wins over UserId. Icon string? An asset ID for a small icon at the end of the row. Value number or string A stat shown at the end of the row.

docs.title: Teams
docs.text: Teams is a list of teams, each with a Name, a Color and its Players. The header takes the colour of the team and shows its name and how many players it has. Press a header and the rows of that team fold away. Give a team a Collapsed Value to fold it yourself. A team with an empty Name has no header, and Players is a shortcut for one such team.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text: A row slides in from the edge and grows to its height when a player joins, and shrinks away when one leaves. Hovering a row fades the display name out while it slides to the left, and brings in @username the same way. With Open set to false the list slides off the edge of the screen.

docs.title: From the experience
docs.text:
Game.Roster builds the Teams for you from the players and teams of the experience. It follows players joining and leaving, team changes, and shows a friend or Premium icon. It uses Players, Teams and the Hidden attribute of a team to leave one out. Players with no team are put in "No Team", and without any teams there is one list without headers.

local roster = Game.Roster(scope, {
    Value = function(player)
        return player:GetAttribute("Kills")
    end,
})

Game.Leaderboard(scope, {
    Teams = roster.Teams,
    Self = roster.Self,
})

Roster takes Value, a function from a player to a stat, and Icon, a function from a player to an icon asset ID.

TopBar is a row of round icon buttons docked to the top left and top right of the screen, as in the Roblox top bar. A button can have a badge and can be highlighted while its panel is open.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text: Pantheon helps in three ways: the theme follows the accessibility settings of the player, the controls can be used from the keyboard and a gamepad, and a helper checks the contrast of your colours.

docs.title: Settings of the player
docs.text:
When you make a theme with Theme.create, Pantheon reads the settings of the player and applies them to the theme. This is on by default. Pass RespectAccessibility = false to turn it off.

Setting Effect ReduceMotion Springs become almost instant and the press scale is removed. PreferredTransparency A low value makes scrims more opaque. The value is from 0 to 1. HighContrast Surfaces and text move towards their extremes. PreferredTextSize The sizes of the type scales are multiplied by 1 for "Medium", 1.15 for "Large", 1.3 for "Larger" and 1.5 for "Largest".

ReduceMotion, PreferredTransparency and PreferredTextSize are read from UserGameSettings.ReducedMotion, GuiService.PreferredTransparency and the preferred text size of the player. HighContrast is not read from the system, so it is only on when you give it.

docs.title: Setting them yourself
docs.text:
To use fixed settings, for a storybook or a test, give them to Theme.create:

local theme = Pantheon.Theme.create("Light", {
    Accessibility = {
        ReduceMotion = true,
        PreferredTransparency = 0.2,
        PreferredTextSize = "Large",
    },
})

You can also apply settings to a theme you already have:

local adjusted = Pantheon.Accessibility.apply(theme, { HighContrast = true })

Accessibility.apply returns a copy of the theme. Accessibility.read returns the settings of the player. Accessibility.motionSpeed(theme, multiplier) returns the spring speed of the theme times multiplier, or the speed of the theme alone when reduced motion is on, for animation of your own.

docs.title: Keyboard and gamepad
docs.text:
Every control that reacts to input, such as buttons, switches, checkboxes, radio buttons, segmented controls, menu rows, list rows and the keypoints of a curve editor, can take focus. Text fields can too.

Key What it does Tab, Shift+Tab Moves focus to the next or previous control, in reading order: top to bottom, then left to right. Enter, Space Activates the focused control, as a click does. Arrow keys On a slider, change the value by one step. Home and End jump to the ends. On a segmented control, move to the next segment. On a split pane divider, move the divider. In the Explorer, move through the tree. Escape Closes the open dialog, sheet, drawer, popover, menu, select or radial menu. The gamepad B button does the same.

The focused control is drawn with a ring, in place of the white box Roblox draws. On a gamepad, focus is Roblox's own GuiService.SelectedObject, so the thumbstick and the D-pad move it and the A button activates the control.

docs.title: Dialogs and sheets
docs.text: While a dialog, an app sheet, a navigation drawer or a popover is open, Tab stays inside it. Focus moves to its first control when it opens, and goes back to where it was when it closes.

docs.title: In your own components
docs.text:
Focus is the module behind this. A control you make yourself joins in with one call:

Pantheon.Focus.manage(myButton, theme)

Enter and Space then activate it by running the handler you gave to OnEvent("Activated").

docs.title: Contrast
docs.text:
Accessibility.audit checks a theme against WCAG 2.1 AA. Text on the colour it is drawn on needs a contrast ratio of 4.5, and controls and their borders need 3:

for _, finding in Pantheon.Accessibility.audit(theme) do
    if not finding.Ok then
        print(`{finding.Foreground} on {finding.Background}: {finding.Ratio}`)
    end
end

The default themes pass for text. The soft Outline colour has a ratio of about 1.7 on Surface, which is below 3 on purpose, since the thin borders it draws are decoration next to a fill. Turn on HighContrast and it becomes a strong line. If your design uses Outline as the only sign that an input is there, use a darker colour for it.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text: Roblox has no screen reader support for custom interface, so the components cannot name themselves to a screen reader. The things above, keyboard use, focus, motion, text size and contrast, are what can be done.

docs.title: Common properties
docs.text:
Most components accept the properties below. A component page lists them only when the component uses them.

Name Type Description Theme ThemeRef Theme for this component, instead of the one from Theme.Provide. It can be a theme or a state of one. LayoutOrder UsedAs<number> Position in a parent UIListLayout or UIGridLayout. Size UsedAs<UDim2> Size. Each component has its own default. Visible UsedAs<boolean> Whether the component is shown. ZIndex UsedAs<number> Z index. Layer Instance Where floating content is mounted. See Overlay layers. Id string Names the component so it can find its state again after a rebuild. See Persisting state.

docs.title: UsedAs<T>
docs.text: UsedAs<T> is the Fusion type for a value that can be a T or a state that holds a T. A property of this type follows a state when you give one.

docs.title: Values you can follow
docs.text:
A control that lets the user change a value, such as Checkbox, Switch, Slider, Select, Tabs, TextField and ColorPicker, keeps that value in its own state. What the property does depends on what you give it:

  • A plain value, such as Checked = true, is the starting value. The control keeps its own state from then on.
  • A Value is linked to the control in both directions. Setting the Value moves the control, and the user changing the control sets the Value.
  • A Computed cannot be set, so it only moves the control. The control still changes when the user uses it, and the next change of the Computed overrides that.
local volume = scope:Value(40)

C.Slider(scope, { Min = 0, Max = 100, Value = volume })

volume:set(75) -- the slider moves

Use the callback of the component, which is OnChanged for most of them, when you want to run code on a change.

A control whose value you link this way is not kept across rebuilds, since you own that state.

docs.title: Properties that are read once
docs.text: Where a property is described as read once, changing the state later has no effect. Disabled is read once on most components.

docs.title: Customising the HUD
docs.text:
This guide shows how to change the Hotbar. Each section is a separate change. Start with this bar:

local items = scope:Value({})

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    Slots = 9,
    Capacity = 27,
})

docs.title: Change the number of slots
docs.text:
Slots is the number of slots on the bar. You can have up to 10, one for each number key. Capacity is the total number of slots. The slots after the first Slots appear only in the inventory panel.

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    Slots = 6, -- (1)!
    Capacity = 24,
    Columns = 6, -- (2)!
    ExpandedRows = 3, -- (3)!
})
  1. The bar has 6 slots. The keys 1 to 6 equip them.
  2. The panel has 6 slots in each row.
  3. The panel shows 3 rows. It scrolls if there are more.

docs.title: Change the size
docs.text:
SlotSize is the width and height of a slot, in pixels. The panel uses the same size.

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    SlotSize = 64,
})

docs.title: Keep the default Roblox backpack
docs.text:
The bar hides the default Roblox backpack. To show both, set DisableDefault to false.

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    DisableDefault = false,
})

docs.title: Handle the keys yourself
docs.text:
Set BindKeys to false to turn off the number keys and the backtick key. Then equip slots and open the panel from your own code:

local selected = scope:Value(nil)
local expanded = scope:Value(false)

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    Selected = selected,
    Expanded = expanded,
    BindKeys = false,
})

UserInputService.InputBegan:Connect(function(input, processed)
    if processed then
        return
    end
    if input.KeyCode == Enum.KeyCode.Tab then -- (1)!
        expanded:set(not peek(expanded))
    end
end)
  1. This opens and closes the panel with the Tab key. You can use any key.

Warning

If you turn off BindKeys, keyboard players cannot equip a slot unless you set Selected yourself. They can still click a slot.

docs.title: Search by your own fields
docs.text:
The search matches any string field of an item. To let players search one field by name, add a scope:

Pantheon.Game.Hotbar(scope, {
    Items = items,
    SearchScopes = {
        rarity = function(item)
            return item.Rarity
        end,
    },
})

A player can now type rarity:epic to match only the rarity.

docs.title: Overlay layers
docs.text: Dialogs, menus, popovers, tooltips, sheets, coach marks and toasts float over the rest of the interface. If they were built inside a layout, they would push their neighbours around. Pantheon mounts them on a layer instead: a transparent frame that covers the area they may appear in.

docs.title: Giving a component a layer
docs.text:
Pass the layer in the Layer property:

local overlayLayer = scope:Frame({
    Name = "OverlayLayer",
    BackgroundTransparency = 1,
    Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1),
    ZIndex = 50,
})

C.Dialog(scope, {
    Layer = overlayLayer,
    Open = open,
    Title = "Delete file?",
})

The layer must be a GuiObject. Put it above your content, usually as the last child of your root frame.

docs.title: A layer for a whole build
docs.text:
Layer.Provide sets the layer for every component created while its function runs, so you do not have to pass it each time:

Pantheon.Layer.Provide(overlayLayer, function()
    C.Dialog(scope, { Open = open, Title = "Delete file?" })
    C.Tooltip(scope, { Target = button, Text = "Delete" })
end)

docs.title: Layers and windows
docs.text: A Window makes a layer inside itself and mounts its Overlays there, so floating content moves with the window and follows its rounded corners. When a Window is created, it also sets its layer as the fallback for components that are created after it and that were not given a layer. Components that are created before the Window do not get it, so pass Layer to those.

docs.title: When there is no layer
docs.text:
A component that needs a layer and cannot find one does one of these:

  • Tooltip and the tooltips of GradientPicker are not shown.
  • Coachmark warns that no overlay layer was found.

See Layer.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Pantheon builds each component once. After that, Fusion states carry the changes. Your interface stays fast if you keep it that way. This page lists what costs time and what you can do about it.

docs.title: Measure first
docs.text: Open DevTools and use the profiler to see which elements change every frame. Use the MicroProfiler in Studio to see what the scripts cost. Fix what you find there before you change anything else.

docs.title: Lifetime checks
docs.text:
Fusion can check that a scope lasts at least as long as the things that read from it. It runs the check on every use and scans the whole scope each time, so it is slow in a large interface. Pantheon turns it off.

Turn it on only when you are looking for a scope that is destroyed too early:

Pantheon.Flags.LifetimeChecks = true

See Flags.

docs.title: Long lists
docs.text: A list builds one instance for every row. Use VirtualList when a list has more than about 100 rows. It builds only the rows you can see. The inventory panel of the Hotbar already does this.

docs.title: Changing theme
docs.text:
By default, a theme change rebuilds the interface. Use Persist so the user keeps what they entered.

Flags.ReactiveTheme is an experimental option. With it, components follow the theme as it changes and nothing is rebuilt. A few colours are still read once, so check your interface in both modes. See Theming.

docs.title: Hidden interface
docs.text: Do not keep hidden interface running. Build an overlay when it opens, or set Visible to false and stop any springs that drive it. A spring that has settled costs nothing. A spring that follows a value that keeps changing costs a step every frame.

docs.title: Fewer states
docs.text: A Computed runs again each time something it reads changes. Put properties that change together in one Computed. Do not return a new table from a Computed each time, because Fusion counts that as a change.

docs.title: Persisting state
docs.text:
The values a user enters, such as the selected tab, a switch, a slider or the text of a field, live in Fusion values inside each component. When you rebuild the interface, for example to change theme or layout, those values are gone with the old components.

Persist keeps them. You give the app a store, and the values live in the scope of the store, so a rebuild finds them again.

docs.title: Using a store
docs.text:
local store = Pantheon.Persist.createStore(rootScope) -- (1)!

local function rebuild()
    Pantheon.Persist.Provide(store, function()
        -- build the interface: every Switch, Tabs, Slider... reuses its value
    end)
end
  1. The store keeps its values in rootScope, so they outlive the scopes of the individual builds.

Without a store, every component creates its own plain values, as usual.

docs.title: How a component finds its value
docs.text:
A component looks up its state:

  • by its Id, when it has one: Id = "settings.sound";
  • otherwise by its kind and the order it was created in during the build: the third Switch is Switch#3.

A rebuild runs the same code in the same order, so the order is stable. Interface that changes the order, such as a switch that is only built when a condition holds, should have explicit Ids.

docs.title: What is not kept
docs.text: A property you give as a state is left alone. If you pass Value = someValue, you own that state, and the component does not store it.

docs.title: Components that keep state
docs.text:
Switch, Checkbox, RadioGroup, ChoiceGroup, Select, MultiSelect, Slider, RangeSlider, DatePicker, TimePicker, Tabs, SegmentedControl, Collapsible, TreeView, StarRating, Pagination, NavigationRail, TextField (the text typed into it), ColorPicker and GradientPicker.

See Persist for the functions.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text: Some parts of Pantheon work in a way you might not expect. This page explains why.

docs.title: A plain value is a starting value
docs.text:
Many properties accept a plain value or a Fusion state. For the value of a control, a plain value is only where the control starts.

  • Give the control a Value and it stays in step with it both ways. When the user changes the control, the Value changes. When you set the Value, the control changes.
  • Give it a Computed and it follows the Computed. The user's changes do not write back.

Every control works like this. See Common properties.

docs.title: Components read the theme once
docs.text:
A component reads its colours, fonts and spacing when you build it. That keeps components small, but it means a theme change normally needs a rebuild of the interface.

A rebuild would lose what the user typed, so Pantheon has Persist. It keeps the state of controls between rebuilds.

docs.title: Components handle focus and motion
docs.text: Each component that takes input draws its own focus ring. It works with a keyboard and a gamepad. It also follows the player's settings for reduced motion and transparency. You do not need to add any of this. See Accessibility.

docs.title: Game components are separate
docs.text: The Game components are styled for a HUD and do not use the app theme. Most games do not want the inventory bar to turn white when the player picks the light theme. Keeping the two sets apart means a change to one does not affect the other.

docs.title: Components are ordinary instances
docs.text: A component returns a normal Roblox instance. You can pass other Fusion properties to it with Apply. If Pantheon does not have the component you need, build it from instances and place it next to the others.

docs.title: Theming
docs.text: A theme is a table with the colours, fonts, type scales, spacing and motion of the interface. Components read from it, so changing the theme changes the whole interface.

docs.title: Making a theme
docs.text:
local theme = Pantheon.Theme.create("Light") -- or "Dark"

Theme.create takes the mode and a table of options:

Option Type Description RespectAccessibility boolean? Read the accessibility settings of the player and apply them. true by default. See Accessibility. Accessibility AccessibilityPrefs? Use these settings instead of reading them. Useful for storybooks and tests. Controls ThemeControls? Settings for controls, such as SwitchIcons. Overrides { [string]: any }? Values to merge over the finished theme. Palette { [string]: ... }? Extra named colours for Color properties. A value is a Color3, a hex string or a full ThemeColorRole. Typography { [string]: TypeScale }? Extra or replaced type scales. The defaults that are not replaced are kept.

docs.title: What is in a theme
docs.text: Field Contents Mode "Light" or "Dark". Colors Roles such as Primary, OnPrimary, Surface, OnSurface, Outline, Error. Each On role is the colour of content drawn on its base. Palette Named colours for Color properties. Each has a Base, an OnBase, a Container and an OnContainer. Fonts Heading, Body and Mono. Typography Scales with a Font, a Size and a LineHeight: Display, Headline, Title, Button, Body, Label and Mono. Metrics Spacing (SpaceXs to SpaceXl), corner radii (RadiusXs to Radius3xl, RadiusPanel, RadiusPill) and sizes such as AppBarHeight, DrawerWidth and RailWidth. Motion SpringSpeed, SpringDamping and PressScale, used by the springs of the components. Icons, Audio Names of icons and sounds. Controls Settings for controls. Accessibility The accessibility settings that were applied, if any.

docs.title: Providing the theme
docs.text:
Theme.Provide makes a theme the current one while a function runs:

Pantheon.Theme.Provide(theme, function()
    C.Button(scope, { Text = "Hello" })
end)

Components find the theme when they are created. To use another theme for one component, pass Theme:

C.Button(scope, { Text = "Hello", Theme = darkTheme })

docs.title: Switching theme
docs.text:
Experimental

With Flags.ReactiveTheme = true, components follow a theme state in place and no rebuild is needed. Pass the state from Theme.createAnimated to Theme.Provide. Colours that are read at build time (a few leftover sites, such as disabled button backgrounds) still show the old theme until rebuilt. With the flag off, use the rebuild approach below.

Components read the theme once, when they are built. A theme change therefore needs a rebuild of the interface. To make a rebuild painless:

  1. Keep the state that matters outside the view, or give the app a Persist store, so controls keep their values.
  2. Build the new interface under the new theme, fade it in over the old one, and then clean up the old one. The demo storyboard does this.

Theme.createAnimated makes a theme state that moves between light and dark with a spring. It is used by the storyboard so that the colours of a new interface start from the old theme and blend over to the new one:

local mode = scope:Value("Light")
local theme = Pantheon.Theme.createAnimated(scope, mode, { Animate = true })

Note

Recolouring a live interface without a rebuild is not supported yet. There are notes on how it could work in Notes.

docs.title: Colours in properties
docs.text:
A property that takes a ColorInput, such as the Color of a Button, accepts:

  • a palette name such as "primary", "secondary" or "error", or a name you added in the Palette option;
  • a Color3;
  • a hex string such as "#00695c";
  • an RGB table such as { 0, 105, 92 };
  • a Material swatch such as "Blue 500" or { Blue = 500 };
  • a full ThemeColorRole.

Anything but a role is turned into a role: a base colour, the colour for content on it, and a container pair.

docs.title: Bind
docs.text:
Bind keeps a control's own state in step with a state you give it. It is how Checkbox, Slider, Select and most other controls follow a Value. See Common properties for what this means for the player of a component.

A control keeps its value in a Value of its own. When you give it a state, link makes the two equal. Setting your state moves the control, and the user changing the control sets your state, as long as it is a Value. A Computed cannot be set, so it only moves the control.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description link: (scope: Scope, prop: any, internal: Value, options: Options?) -> () Links internal to prop. Nothing happens when prop is not a state. linkParts: (scope: Scope, prop: any, parts: { Value }, join: (...any) -> any, split: (value: any) -> { any }?, equals: ((a, b) -> boolean)?) -> () Like link, for a value kept in several Values, such as a range in two ends or a date in year, month and day. join builds your value from the parts and split takes it apart. When split returns nil, the parts are kept. isState: (value: any) -> boolean Whether value is a Fusion state. isWritable: (value: any) -> boolean Whether value is a state that can be set. listEquals: (a: any, b: any) -> boolean Equality for lists of strings or numbers.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Name Description toInternal Converts your state's value to the form the control keeps. toProp Converts the control's value to the form your state holds. equals Compares two values. Needed for tables, since the default is ==. 
local selected = scope:Value("a")
Bind.link(scope, props.Selected, selected)

docs.title: DevTools
docs.text:
DevTools is a panel for looking at a running interface, in the style of React DevTools. It shows the tree of the interface, lets you edit the properties of an element, and shows what changes while the interface runs. It reads the interface of the local player, so it works on any Roblox UI, not only Pantheon's.

Pantheon.Flags.DevTools = true
local unmount = Pantheon.DevTools.mount()

Press F8 to open and close the panel. mount returns a function that removes the tools.

Note

DevTools does nothing, and warns, unless Flags.DevTools is true when you call mount. This keeps it out of a released experience by default.

docs.title: The panel
docs.text: The panel is docked at the bottom of the screen. Drag its top edge to change the height.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The left side is a tree of the interface, an Explorer over the PlayerGui. Type in the search box to filter it. Pointing at a row outlines that element on screen, with its name and size.

The right side is the selected element:

  • Name. Editable.
  • Path. Press an ancestor to select it.
  • Properties. Each has an editor that suits its type: a switch for a boolean, a number field for a number, a text field for text and colours, number fields for a UDim2, a UDim or a Vector2, and a button that steps through the items of an enum. The values follow the element while it changes, and what you edit is written to it at once.
  • Attributes. The attributes of the element.
  • Children. Press one to select it.

The pointer button in the header lets you click an element on screen to select it. Escape leaves it. The tree opens up to the element you picked.

docs.title: Profiler
docs.text: Press Record, use the interface, and the Profiler lists the elements that changed most, with how many changes there were and how many each second. Changes to the layout, such as AbsoluteSize, are not counted. Press an entry to select the element. This shows what is animating or being rewritten more often than it should.

docs.title: Highlight updates
docs.text: The lightning button in the header makes an element flash each time one of its properties changes, as the highlight of React DevTools does. A hot spot flashes all the time. At most thirty elements flash at once.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Switches for Flags.CanvasFade, Flags.LifetimeChecks and Flags.BetaUI. Components read flags when they are built, so rebuild the interface to see the effect.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description mount: (props: Props?) -> () -> () Builds the tools. Returns a function that removes them.

docs.title: Props
docs.text: Name Type Default Description Parent Instance? The PlayerGui Where the ScreenGui of the tools is placed. Hotkey Enum.KeyCode? Enum.KeyCode.F8 Opens and closes the panel. Theme ThemeRef? A dark theme Theme of the tools. By default they have a dark theme of their own, so they look the same in any app. Open boolean? false Open the panel when it is mounted. Height number? 340 Height of the panel in pixels.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Features finds out which newer Roblox UI features the engine has, so a component can use them and fall back to something else when they are missing. A feature is tested once, by creating an instance and setting the property, and the answer is kept.

Flags.BetaUI = false makes the features that are in a beta report false.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Feature individualCorners: () -> boolean UICorner radii for each corner (TopLeftRadius and the others). gradientTypes: () -> boolean UIGradient.Type set to "Radial" or "Conical". Studio beta. gradientTiling: () -> boolean UIGradient tile mode and scale. Studio beta. shadowText: () -> boolean UIShadow in its text mode. Studio beta.

docs.title: Used by
docs.text:
• Window and Overlay round single corners with individualCorners. Without it they keep square corners where they meet.
  • ColorPicker draws the hue ring with gradientTypes, and falls back to a square.
  • Loader, Progress and the arcs they draw use conical gradients when they can.
  • NumberSpinner blurs digits with a text shadow when shadowText is true.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flags are switches for how the library behaves. Set them before you build your interface:

Pantheon.Flags.LifetimeChecks = true

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Name Type Default Description CanvasFade boolean false Wrap chrome that appears, such as dialogs, in a CanvasGroup and fade its GroupTransparency. When it is off, the transparency of each element is faded instead. LifetimeChecks boolean false Run the lifetime checks of Fusion. They scan a whole scope on every use, so they are slow, and Pantheon turns them off. Turn them on to find a scope that outlives what it uses. ReactiveTheme boolean false Let components follow a theme state, so changing the mode updates colours in place instead of needing a rebuild. Experimental. BetaUI boolean true Use UI features that are in Studio betas, such as conical and radial gradients and text shadows, when the engine has them. Set it to false to force the fallbacks. See Features. ConicalRotation number -90 Degrees added to the rotation of a conical gradient so that position 0 is at 12 o'clock. A conical gradient starts at 3 o'clock, so -90 puts the start at the top. Change it if an arc or the colour wheel looks turned. ConicalClockwise boolean true Whether a conical gradient sweeps clockwise.

The storyboard has a calibration ring that fills from 12 o'clock to 3 o'clock. If it is turned or mirrored, adjust ConicalRotation and ConicalClockwise.

docs.title: Focus
docs.text: Focus manages keyboard and gamepad focus. The components use it, and you can use it for your own. See Accessibility for what it gives the player.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A control that takes focus is registered with manage. The module then watches GuiService.SelectedObject: when it is a registered control, a ring is drawn around it. Tab moves SelectedObject between the registered controls that are showing.

Enter and Space need the handler of the control's Activated event, and a script cannot fire an event. When the module starts, it wraps the Activated key of Fusion's OnEvent once, and remembers the handler given to each instance. This is why manage works with any control that connects Activated through OnEvent.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description manage: (gui: GuiObject, theme: Theme, textBox: boolean?) -> () Makes gui a control that can take focus. Selectable is turned on and Roblox's own selection box is hidden. Set textBox for an input, so Tab focuses its text. Interaction.wire, which most components call, does this for you. select: (gui: GuiObject?) -> () Moves focus to gui, or clears it for nil. A TextBox also captures the keyboard. onKey: (gui: GuiObject, handler: (input: InputObject) -> boolean) -> () Calls handler for key presses while gui has focus. Return true for a key you used. The arrow keys of a slider are done this way. trap: (scope: Scope, root: GuiObject, open: UsedAs<boolean>) -> () While open is true, Tab stays inside root. Focus moves to the first control in it, and goes back to where it was when open turns false. escape: (scope: Scope, open: UsedAs<boolean>, close: () -> ()) -> () While open is true, Escape and the gamepad B button call close. When several are open, the one opened last closes. closer: (props: { OnClose: (() -> ())?, Open: any }) -> (() -> ()) A function that closes an overlay: it calls OnClose, or sets a Value passed as Open to false.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local button = scope:TextButton({
    Text = "Run",
    [Fusion.OnEvent("Activated")] = run,
})
Pantheon.Focus.manage(button, theme) -- Tab reaches it, Enter and Space call `run`

local open = scope:Value(false)
Pantheon.Focus.trap(scope, panel, open)
Pantheon.Focus.escape(scope, open, function()
    open:set(false)
end)

docs.title: GroupFade
docs.text:
GroupFade fades an instance and everything under it by driving the transparency of each element. It does this without a CanvasGroup, which would draw the group to a texture, use more memory, make text softer and clip anything that spills outside it, such as shadows and strokes.

Every element gets the same multiplier, so an opaque panel, its text, icons, strokes and shadows fade together:

transparency = 1 - (1 - base) × alpha

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Name Description bind: (scope: Scope, root: Instance, alpha: State<number>) -> () Fades root and its descendants with alpha. 0 is invisible and 1 is shown. Instances added to root later are included. The binding ends when the scope is cleaned up. 
local reveal = scope:Spring(scope:Value(0), 20, 1)
Pantheon.GroupFade.bind(scope, panel, reveal)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each time alpha changes, GroupFade compares the transparency of each element with the value it wrote last time. If they differ, something else changed it, for example a hover effect, and the new value becomes the base. Then it writes the faded value. When alpha reaches 1 it puts the exact base values back and stops tracking, so a group that is fully visible costs nothing.

An element can opt out by setting the attribute PantheonNoFade to true.

Warning

Do not bind two GroupFades to instances where one is inside the other. They would see each other's writes as changes made by something else and the base values would drift.

docs.title: Layer
docs.text: Layer says where floating content is mounted. See Overlay layers.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description Provide: (layer: GuiObject, callback: (...) -> ..., ...) -> ... Makes layer the current layer while callback runs. It is also remembered as the fallback layer. bind: (layer: Instance?) -> () Sets the fallback layer, used by components that are created when there is no current layer. A Window calls it for its own overlay layer. Pass nil to clear it. use: () -> GuiObject? The current layer, or the fallback layer. resolve: (props: { Layer: Instance? }?) -> GuiObject? The Layer of props if it is a GuiObject, and use() otherwise. mount: (scope: Scope, props, instance: Instance) -> boolean Parents instance to the resolved layer, and removes it again when the scope is cleaned up. It returns false, and leaves instance alone, when there is no layer. asGui: (instance: Instance?) -> GuiObject? instance if it is a GuiObject.

docs.text: Name Description Contextual The Fusion Contextual that holds the current layer.

docs.text: Name Description Components The components. Each is a function (scope, props) -> Instance. Game The in-game components: TopBar, Hotbar and Backpack. See Hotbar. Theme Making and providing themes. See Theme. Style Reusable defaults for components. See Style. Persist Keeping component state across rebuilds. See Persist. Layer The overlay layer of an interface. See Layer. Flags Switches for library behaviour. See Flags. Validators Validators for form fields. See Validators. Accessibility Reading and applying accessibility settings. See the Accessibility guide. GroupFade Fades an instance and everything under it. See GroupFade. CanvasFade Helpers that fade panels with a CanvasGroup, or with GroupFade when the flag is off. docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description scoped: () -> Scope Makes a Fusion scope that has the Fusion methods and the instance methods of Iona. scope:Apply(instance) is available on it too, and scope:Hydrate is an alias for it.

docs.title: Types
docs.text: The module also exports the types Theme, ThemeMode, Scope, ButtonProps, TextFieldProps, ListItemProps, ButtonVariant, ColorInput, ThemeColorRole and ThemePalette.

docs.title: Persist
docs.text: Persist keeps the state of components across rebuilds of an interface. Persisting state explains the idea.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Name Description createStore: (scope: Scope) -> Store Makes a store. Its values live in scope, so they last as long as it does. Provide: (store: Store, build: (...) -> ..., ...) -> ... Makes store the current store while build runs, and returns what it returns. The counters that name components start again, so the same code finds the same state. If build errors, the store is restored and the error is raised again. key: (kind: string, id: string?, controlled: boolean?) -> string? The key of a component: id, or kind and the number of the component in this build. It is nil when there is no store, or when controlled is true. value: (scope: Scope, key: string?, slot: string, initial: any) -> Value The value for one piece of a component's state. It is the stored one when the key has one, and a new Value otherwise. initial is only used the first time.

key and value are for the components. You only need them to give your own component this behaviour:

local key = Persist.key("MyToggle", props.Id)
local on = Persist.value(scope, key, "on", false)

docs.title: Style
docs.text: Style has two jobs: tokens that read from the current theme, and reusable defaults for components.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
The tokens are tables that look up the current theme each time you read a field:

Name Reads from Example Color theme.Colors Style.Color.Primary Font theme.Fonts Style.Font.Heading Type theme.Typography Style.Type.Title.Size Space spacing in theme.Metrics Style.Space.Md Radius corner radii in theme.Metrics Style.Radius.Lg

docs.title: Layout presets
Defining a style
docs.text:
A style is a set of default properties, either a table or a function of the theme. define makes one. Several specs are layered, and later ones win.

local Style = Pantheon.Style

local Primary = Style.define({ Variant = "Filled" })
local Danger = Primary:extend(function(theme)
    return { Color = theme.Colors.Error }
end)

A style has these methods:

Name Description resolve: (self) -> Props The properties of the style, resolved against the current theme. extend: (self, spec) -> StyleDef A new style made of this one and spec. spec wins. apply: (self, props) -> Props props merged over the style, so props wins.

docs.title: Styled components
docs.text:
styled makes a copy of a component that uses a style as its defaults. The properties you give when you call it win:

local PrimaryButton = Style.styled(Pantheon.Components.Button, Primary)

PrimaryButton(scope, { Text = "Run" })

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description define: (...Spec) -> StyleDef Makes a style. styled: (component, style) -> component Makes a component that has style as its defaults. merge: (...Props) -> Props Merges property tables from left to right. Later ones win, except children, which are joined. deepMerge: (base, over) -> Props Merges over into base. Plain tables merge field by field. Arrays, instances and states are replaced.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: Theme makes the tables that components read their look from, and says which one is current. See Theming for what a theme holds and how to switch it.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Name Description create: (mode: ThemeMode?, opts: ThemeCreateOpts?) -> Theme Makes a theme. mode is "Light" or "Dark", and is "Light" when left out. createAnimated: (scope: Scope, mode: UsedAs<ThemeMode>, opts: { Animate: boolean?, ... }?) -> ThemeRef Makes a state of a theme that follows mode. When the mode changes, the theme blends from one to the other with a spring. Set Animate = false, or turn on reduced motion, and it swaps at once. Provide: (theme: ThemeRef, callback: (...) -> ..., ...) -> ... Makes theme the current theme while callback runs, and returns what it returns. use: () -> Theme The current theme. It fails if there is none. useRef: () -> ThemeRef Like use, but returns the state when the theme was provided as one. resolve: (props: { Theme: ThemeRef? }?) -> Theme The Theme of props if it has one, and the current theme otherwise. Components use it. blend: (a: Theme, b: Theme, t: number) -> Theme A theme between two others. t is from 0 to 1. deepMerge: (base: any, over: any) -> any Merges over into base. Tables merge field by field. Other values are replaced.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Name Description Contextual The Fusion Contextual that holds the current theme. Accessibility The Accessibility module. Color The colour helpers. Material The Material colour swatches.

Note

Provide also remembers the theme as a fallback. A function that Fusion runs later, such as the callback of a Computed, has lost the context, and finds the last provided theme instead.

docs.title: Validators
docs.text:
A validator is a function that checks a value and returns whether it is valid, and a message when it is not:

type Validator = (value: any) -> (boolean, string?)

TextField, ChoiceGroup, Select and MultiSelect take a list of them in Validators. They are checked in order, and the first one that fails shows its message.

local V = Pantheon.Validators

C.TextField(scope, {
    Label = "Username",
    Validators = { V.required(), V.minLength(3), V.maxLength(20) },
})

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Each function that makes a validator takes an optional message, which replaces the default.

Name Passes when Default message required(message?) The value is not nil, an empty string or an empty list. Required minLength(n, message?) The text has at least n characters. At least n characters maxLength(n, message?) The text has at most n characters. At most n characters email(message?) The text looks like an email address. An empty text passes. Enter a valid email pattern(pattern, message?) The text matches a Luau pattern. An empty text passes. Invalid format numberRange(min?, max?, message?) The value is a number between min and max. Out of range all(list) Every validator in list passes. The message of the first that fails run(list?, value) Returns the result of the first validator in list that fails, or true when they all pass.

An empty text passes email and pattern, so a field that may be left empty does not need a special case. Add required for a field that may not be.

docs.title: Installing Pantheon
docs.text:
Pantheon is on Wally. Add it to your wally.toml and run wally install:

[dependencies]
Pantheon = "koterahq/pantheon@0.1.0"

Wally installs the libraries Pantheon needs too. To run the demo, or to work on Pantheon itself, install it from the repository as below.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Pantheon needs these libraries. Wally installs them.

Library Version Used for Fusion 0.3.0 State and instances Iona (koterahq/iona) 0.3.0 Short forms for properties such as CornerRadius and Layout Lucide icons 0.1.3 The icons of Icon, IconButton and others Snapdragon 2.0.0 Dragging

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Clone the repository. In it, run:

rokit install
wally install
rojo serve demo.project.json

rokit install installs Rojo, Wally, StyLua and Selene at the versions in rokit.toml. wally install fills the Packages folder. rojo serve syncs the project with Studio.

Open demo.rbxlx in Studio and connect the Rojo plugin. Press Play to run the storyboard. It shows every component in light and dark mode.

docs.title: Using it in your own project
docs.text:
Add the src folder to your Rojo project as Pantheon, next to the packages it needs:

{
    "name": "my-game",
    "tree": {
        "$className": "DataModel",
        "ReplicatedStorage": {
            "Packages": {
                "$path": "Packages",
                "Pantheon": { "$path": "../pantheon/src" }
            }
        }
    }
}

Then require it in a client script:

local Pantheon = require(ReplicatedStorage.Packages.Pantheon)

Next, build an interface.

docs.title: Using Pantheon
docs.text: This page builds a small interface. You need to know the basics of Fusion: values, computeds and scopes. If you do not, read the Fusion tutorials first.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Fusion keeps everything it creates in a scope, and destroys it when you clean the scope up. Pantheon has its own scoped. It gives you the usual Fusion methods and the instance methods from Iona, such as scope:Frame:

local Pantheon = require(Packages.Pantheon)
local Fusion = Pantheon.Fusion
local C = Pantheon.Components

local scope = Pantheon.scoped()

docs.title: The theme
docs.text:
Components take their look from a theme. Build your interface inside Theme.Provide:

local theme = Pantheon.Theme.create("Dark")

Pantheon.Theme.Provide(theme, function()
    -- build the interface here
end)

If you leave this out, creating a component fails with the error Pantheon.Theme.Provide required. To give one component its own theme, use its Theme property. See Theming.

docs.title: A component
docs.text:
A component is a function. It takes a scope and a table of properties, and returns an instance:

local save = C.Button(scope, {
    Text = "Save",
    Variant = "Filled",
    OnClick = function()
        print("Saved")
    end,
})

A property of type UsedAs<T> takes a plain value or a Fusion state. If you give it a state, the component follows the state:

local name = scope:Value("Ada")

C.Text(scope, {
    Text = scope:Computed(function(use)
        return "Hello, " .. use(name)
    end),
})

name:set("Grace") -- the text changes

Controls that the user changes, such as Slider and Checkbox, work both ways. A plain value sets only the starting value. A Value stays in step with the control. See Common properties.

docs.title: Putting it on screen
docs.text:
A component returns an ordinary instance. Put it in a ScreenGui:

local gui = scope:New("ScreenGui")({
    Name = "App",
    ResetOnSpawn = false,
    Parent = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui"),
    [Fusion.Children] = {
        C.Window(scope, {
            AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5),
            Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5),
            Size = UDim2.fromOffset(480, 320),
            AppBar = C.AppBar(scope, { Title = "My app" }),
            Children = { save },
        }),
    },
})

docs.title: Cleaning up
docs.text:
Cleaning up the scope destroys everything in it:

Fusion.doCleanup(scope)

To rebuild an interface, for example when the theme changes, make a new inner scope for each build and clean up the old one. Persisting state shows how to keep what the user entered.
